entities.name: National Geographic Society
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National Geographic Society, founded in Washington D.C. in 1888 'for the increase and diffusion of geographic knowledge,' is one of the world's largest nonprofit scientific and educational institutions — funding 15,000+ research, exploration, and conservation projects, publishing the National Geographic magazine (since 1888, 35 million global circulation at peak), producing iconic wildlife photography, and now operating National Geographic cable channels and streaming through a Disney majority partnership. The yellow-bordered magazine cover is one of the most recognized design elements in publishing history.

National Geographic's founding membership of 33 geographers, explorers, and scientists grew rapidly after Gilbert Grosvenor (editor 1899-1954) introduced photographic illustration — revolutionary for 1900s magazines — making geographic exploration visual and accessible. The magazine's photography — from Luis Marden's 1956 discovery of the Bounty wreck, to the 1984 'Afghan Girl' portrait, to Jane Goodall's chimpanzee photos — created icons of environmental consciousness and cultural encounter.

National Geographic's scientific contributions include: funding Robert Peary's (disputed) 1909 North Pole expedition, Jacques Cousteau's undersea films, Richard Leakey's Kenyan fossil discoveries, and Jane Goodall's chimpanzee research. The 1984 'Afghan Girl' (Sharbat Gula, photographed by Steve McCurry) is the most recognized magazine cover photograph ever taken. National Geographic's partnership with Disney (launched 2019, 73% Disney ownership) merged it with Disney's streaming strategy while the Society retains its scientific grant-making mission through the National Geographic Foundation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: National Geographic Society's marriage of scientific exploration and photographic storytelling — from Peary's North Pole to Goodall's chimpanzees to the Afghan Girl — created the world's most powerful visual record of geographic and environmental knowledge, making exploration emotionally accessible to millions.
